passage:
I'm Bhupen, on the product team with Ishita. Last month we argued for a week about whether customers want a saved-lists feature. Half the team said yes and half said it was clutter.
In the meeting Ishita said, "We could argue until December. Let's ask twelve real users." Nobody had suggested that. Ishita built a rough version in three days and sent it to a small group. Six used it twice, four never opened it, and two wrote long comments.
I don't know if Ishita felt sure, but the argument stopped, because there was something on the table we could all read. We changed the feature the following week.

qa.q: How many users were asked to try the feature?
What might Ishita have felt when proposing the test?
qa.a: Bhupen cannot tell whether Ishita felt sure, but Ishita seems impatient with the long argument and eager for real evidence.

qa.q: What could the team do if the test results were mixed?
qa.a: They could run a second small test with a changed version, since only real use will settle what users want.

qa.q: How did the users in the small group take part in the decision?
qa.a: Six used the feature twice, four never opened it and two wrote long comments, so their actions gave the team something to read instead of opinions.

grounding: A product team unsure whether customers want a feature runs a small test with a few users instead of debating.

passage:
Monday: The argument had run for forty minutes. Ramesh was sure customers wanted a button to reorder last week's groceries; Neha from design was sure they'd never touch it. Jatin finally raised a hand. "We could debate this all month. None of us is a customer."
Thursday: Ramesh built a rough version in a day and a half. Jatin picked twenty regular users, quietly switched it on only for them, and set a reminder to check in a week. "We watch what they do, not what we think they'll do."
The next Thursday: eleven of the twenty had tapped the button, and four had used it twice. Two had written in, confused that it added things they'd already bought. Ramesh grinned at the first number, then frowned at the second. "So they want it, but not like this," he said. Jatin nodded. "Now we know what to fix."

qa.q: How many of the twenty users tapped the button?
qa.a: Eleven of the twenty had tapped the button.

qa.q: Why did Jatin stop the Monday argument?
qa.a: Jatin was frustrated that forty minutes of debate had settled nothing, and felt sure only real customers' behaviour could answer the question.

qa.q: What small step would help before switching it on for everyone?
qa.a: Fix the confusion about items already bought and test again with a fresh small group, so the team knows the fix works.

qa.q: What is it like for Ramesh when the results come in?
qa.a: Ramesh is pleased that people used the button but uneasy about the confused messages, seeing that the idea needs changes.

grounding: Shows a product team settling a debate about a new button by trying it with a few real users over two weeks.

passage: Hrithik, you want to argue with the sales team for another week? Sit with old Vishal for a minute. When I was about twenty-five, I worked at a small company making billing software for clinics. Our boss wanted a feature that sent patients a reminder text before their visit. Half the room said clinics would love it; half said they'd switch it off. We argued for two weeks. Then a quiet tester called Sunanda said, "Why don't we ask five clinics to try it for a month?" So we did. Three kept it on. Two switched it off in the first week, because patients complained about messages arriving late at night. That one detail, the timing, we would never have guessed in a meeting room. We fixed it before launch. So pick a few real users, Hrithik, and let them settle the argument for you.

qa.q: What feature did the boss want?
qa.a: A feature that sent patients a reminder text before their visit.

qa.q: What was the young Vishal likely feeling during the two weeks of arguing?
qa.a: Vishal was probably frustrated and stuck, since the room was split in half and talk alone could not settle it.

qa.q: Why was Sunanda's suggestion a turning point in the story?
qa.a: Asking five clinics to try it for a month replaced guesses with real use, and it uncovered the timing problem nobody had thought of in meetings.

qa.q: How might the two clinics that switched the feature off have seen it?
qa.a: They were likely annoyed, because their patients complained about late-night messages, so the feature felt like a nuisance rather than a help.

grounding: Shows, in a senior colleague's memory, a team testing a reminder feature with a few clinics instead of debating, because only real use could settle it.
